entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a guess or feeling that you can't fully explain, based on small signs or intuition rather than clear evidence.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, followed by a clause with or without *that*. It often has a knowing or humorous tone when the signs are obvious: *Something tells me he forgot.* It sounds more playful than *I have a feeling*, so it is rare in formal writing.
examples: The dog's hiding under the bed. **Something tells me** he's the one who ate the cake.
**Something tells me** we're not getting out of this meeting before six.
Ten missed calls from my sister? **Something tells me** she saw the photos from the party.

drill.sentence: Mom's cleaning the whole house and baking bread. {{Something tells me}} Grandma's coming to visit.
drill.hint: an inner voice suggests, from the signs (not *I have a feeling* or *I bet*)

entries.related: *I have a feeling* — same idea, more neutral; *I bet* — more confident, casual; *my gut tells me* — stresses instinct over evidence.

entries.label: understatement
entries.meaning: Signals that the words you just used are gentler than the truth: the real situation is much worse or more extreme.
entries.usage: Usually added after the description, between commas or at the end: *The trip was a disaster, to put it mildly.* It is common in speech and writing, often with dry humor. *That's putting it mildly* is a typical reply when someone else describes something too gently.
examples: Our first apartment was small, **to put it mildly** — you could cook dinner from the bed.
"Was your boss upset?" "Upset is **putting it mildly**. He was furious."
Grandpa's driving has gotten a little adventurous, **to put it mildly**.

drill.sentence: My brother isn't very organized, {{to put it mildly}}. He once showed up to his own wedding without the rings.
drill.hint: said gently; the truth is much worse (not *to say the least*)

entries.related: *to say the least* — very similar and usually interchangeable; *that's an understatement* — a reply saying something was described too gently; *not exactly* — ironic understatement: *It's not exactly cheap.*

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Says that the reasoning behind your last point also applies to the next one, often pointing in the other direction.
entries.usage: Common in careful speech, opinion writing and debate, at the start of a sentence or after *and*, *but* or *then*. It makes an argument sound fair and balanced, because the same principle is applied both ways. It can sound a little formal in casual chat, where people often say *the same goes for* … instead.
examples: If we blame the coach for the losses, then **by the same token** we should give him credit for the wins.
Kids need clear limits. **By the same token**, they need room to make their own mistakes.
A small study can't prove the drug works; **by the same token**, it can't prove that it doesn't.

drill.sentence: If you get a bonus when sales go up, then {{by the same token}}, you can't complain when there's no bonus in a bad year.
drill.hint: following identical reasoning, fairly in both directions (not *by that logic* or *by the … logic*)

entries.related: *by that logic* — follows someone's reasoning, often to show it fails; *likewise* — more formal, simply means *also*; *conversely* — introduces the reverse case, formal.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a second point that balances or partly contradicts the first, while both remain true; close to *but on the other hand*.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, at the start of a sentence or after *but*. In this sense nothing happens simultaneously; the speaker weighs two sides of one view. It sounds thoughtful and fair, so it is useful for softening a refusal or a criticism.
examples: I'm thrilled about the promotion. **At the same time**, I'm nervous about managing my former teammates.
I want my kids to be independent, but **at the same time**, I worry every time they take the subway alone.
The city wants more housing downtown; **at the same time**, residents don't want taller buildings on their street.

drill.sentence: I'm excited about the new house, but {{at the same time}}, I'm really going to miss this neighborhood.
drill.hint: but also — the balancing side of one view (not *on the other hand* or *then again*)

mistake.wrong: The job pays well. In the same time, the hours are very long.
mistake.right: The job pays well. At the same time, the hours are very long.
mistake.why: The fixed phrase is *at the same time*; *in the same time* is a common learner error.

entries.related: *on the other hand* — more structured contrast; *that said* — limits a view you still hold; *then again* — adds doubt to what you just said.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces the opposite side of a situation, usually a disadvantage after an advantage, or an advantage after a disadvantage.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, podcasts and informal writing, usually at the start of a sentence. It is more casual than *on the other hand* and usually compares good and bad effects of the same thing, not two different options. *The flip side* also works as a noun: *the flip side of fame*.
examples: Working from home saves me two hours a day. **On the flip side**, I sometimes don't talk to anyone until dinner.
The new stadium will bring jobs. **On the flip side**, traffic on game days is going to be terrible.
"The rent's really high." "Sure, but **on the flip side**, you can walk to work."

drill.sentence: Living in a small town means everyone knows you. That's nice, but {{on the flip side}}, everyone also knows your business.
drill.hint: looking at the opposite effect, casual style (not *on the other hand*, *at the same time* or *then again*)

entries.related: *on the other hand* — neutral, also for comparing two options; *the downside is* — names only the disadvantage; *then again* — adds doubt rather than a second effect.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a new point that is connected to the current topic but not the same, to move the conversation on smoothly.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, emails, newsletters and podcasts, at the start of a sentence. It signals a small shift, not a full change of topic; for an unrelated point people say *on a different note* or *on another note*. In casual chat it can sound a little like a presenter, which some people use for humor.
examples: Thanks for the update on hiring. **On a related note**, we still need someone to train the new people.
We're getting a puppy next month! **On a related note**, does anyone have a crate we could borrow?
The city is repaving Main Street this summer. **On a related note**, the farmers market will move to Oak Avenue.

drill.sentence: We're driving to the coast for the long weekend. {{On a related note}}, does anyone know a good place to stop for lunch on the way?
drill.hint: introducing a connected point (not *speaking of which* or *by the way*)

entries.related: *speaking of which* — casual, picks up something just mentioned; *on a different note* — moves to an unrelated topic; *by the way* — adds any extra point, often unconnected.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces the most important point, often a problem, a complication or an honest explanation that the listener needs to hear.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation, at work and at home; the speaker usually pauses after it to draw attention. It often comes before an awkward explanation or a refusal, so listeners hear it as a warning that something unwelcome is coming. In writing it sounds chatty.
examples: I'd love to come to the wedding. **Here's the thing**, though: I can't get the time off work.
**Here's the thing** about cheap printers: the ink costs more than the printer.
The model looks great on paper, but **here's the thing** — nobody's tested it on real patients.

drill.sentence: I know you want a dog, and honestly, so do I. But {{here's the thing}}. Our lease doesn't allow pets.
drill.hint: listen, this is the key point (a whole sentence on its own; not *problem*, *catch* or *deal*)

entries.related: *the thing is* — same function, followed directly by a clause; *the bottom line is* — the final, most important fact; *the catch is* — names a hidden problem.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the listener that a surprising or shocking detail is coming, to build up to it in a story.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American storytelling, said just before the surprising part, often after *and*. It shows excitement, amusement or outrage. It is too casual for formal speech, and in writing it appears mainly in chatty texts and blogs.
examples: So I finally called the landlord, and **get this** — he'd already promised our parking spot to someone else.
**Get this**: my grandmother just signed up for skydiving lessons.
Our neighbor's cat has, **get this**, its own Instagram account with fifty thousand followers.

drill.sentence: So the plumber shows up three hours late, and {{get this}}, he didn't even bring his tools.
drill.hint: here comes the shocking detail (not *guess what*, *listen* or *believe it or not*)

entries.related: *guess what* — similar, can also open a conversation; *you won't believe this* — more dramatic; *check this out* — usually about something you can see.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Asks whether other people notice or feel the same thing, while hinting that you think it is true.
entries.usage: A friendly way to start a mild complaint or observation without sounding too sure of it. After *or* comes a second yes/no question with normal question word order (*is it …*, *does he …*, *has she …*). It's casual; in an email to a manager, *Has anyone else noticed …?* is safer.
examples: **Is it just me, or** is it really cold in this office?
Okay, **is it just me, or** did that movie make no sense at all?
I love Sam, but **is it just me, or** has he been really quiet lately?

drill.sentence: {{Is it just me, or}} does this soup taste a little sour?
drill.hint: asking if other people notice it too

mistake.wrong: Is it just me, or this coffee tastes weird?
mistake.right: Is it just me, or does this coffee taste weird?
mistake.why: The part after *or* is a second question, so it needs question word order with *does*, *is*, *are* and so on.

entries.related: *am I the only one who …?* — similar, a bit more direct; *does anyone else think …?* — asks a group, fine in writing.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Asks someone to listen to your whole idea before they judge or reject it, usually because you expect resistance.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk and informal meetings, said right before an idea that sounds strange, risky or unpopular at first; it often follows *just* or *okay*, and it can be playful. *Hear someone out* is also a normal phrasal verb: *At least hear her out.*
examples: Okay, **hear me out**: what if we skipped the hotel and rented a camper van instead?
I know you hate the idea, but just **hear me out** before you say no.
The council agreed to **hear her out** before voting on the new bike lanes.

drill.sentence: I know a peanut butter and pickle sandwich sounds gross, but {{hear me out}}: it's actually amazing.
drill.hint: let me explain fully before you judge (not *trust me* or *listen*)

entries.related: *bear with me* — asks for patience while you finish something; *trust me* — asks for belief, not for listening; *let me finish* — firmer, after an interruption.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks politely why someone thinks or said something, showing interest rather than disagreement.
entries.usage: A neutral, open question used in conversation, interviews and counseling; it invites the person to explain without sounding like a challenge. Compare *Why would you say that?*, which can sound hurt or defensive. Tone still matters: said flatly, it can sound skeptical.
examples: "I don't think Jake is happy at his new job." "Really? **What makes you say that**?"
"This house has had water damage." "**What makes you say that**?" "Look at the stains on the ceiling."
The doctor asked, "**What makes you say** the pain is worse at night?"

drill.sentence: "I have a feeling the new neighbors won't stay long." "Oh? {{What makes you say that}}? Did something happen?"
drill.hint: a curious request for your reasons (not *why …?* or *how …?*)

mistake.wrong: What makes you to say that?
mistake.why: After *make* + object, use the bare infinitive without *to*.

entries.related: *why do you say that?* — similar, a bit more direct; *how do you figure?* — casual, sounds more skeptical; *what are you getting at?* — asks for a hidden point.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks how someone reached a conclusion, usually because it surprises you or you doubt it.
entries.usage: Casual American English, used as a short reply to a claim that seems wrong or strange. It sounds more skeptical than *What makes you say that?*, and with a flat tone it can sound like a challenge. A fuller form is *How do you figure that?*
examples: "We actually saved money by eating out every night." "**How do you figure**?"
"I'd say the Lakers are the favorites this year." "**How do you figure**? They lost their best player."
You think we'll finish the kitchen by Friday? **How do you figure that**?

drill.sentence: "Honestly, this trip is going to be cheaper than staying home." "{{How do you figure}}? The flights alone cost a thousand bucks."
drill.hint: how did you reach that conclusion? (not *how so?* or *what makes you …?*)

entries.related: *how so?* — short, neutral request for an explanation; *what makes you say that?* — more polite and curious; *says who?* — challenges the source, not the reasoning.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks someone to state directly the point they seem to be hinting at.
entries.usage: Used in conversation when someone is being indirect, often with a suspicious or impatient tone, as if you sense a hidden criticism: *What exactly are you getting at?* In *I see what you're getting at*, it is neutral and means you understand the point.
examples: "You've been working late a lot." "**What are you getting at**? You think I'm avoiding you?"
I'm not sure **what you're getting at** — can you just say it plainly?
I think I see **what she was getting at** in the meeting: the team is too small for this project.

drill.sentence: "Your sister got a raise, and she's younger than you." "Okay, {{what are you getting at}}?"
drill.hint: say the point you're hinting at (not *… trying to say*, *… going with this* or *… your point*)

entries.related: *what's your point?* — blunter; *where are you going with this?* — asks where an argument will end up; *what are you implying?* — more formal, suspects an insult.

entries.term: where are you going with this?
entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks what conclusion or request someone is leading up to, when you can't yet see the point of what they are saying.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and meetings when someone gives a long build-up or asks odd questions. Said with curiosity or a laugh, it's friendly; said flatly, it shows impatience or suspicion. A softer form is *I'm not sure where you're going with this*.
examples: "So, are you free Saturday? And do you still have that truck?" "Ha, **where are you going with this**?"
I'm not sure **where you're going with this**, Tom. Can you get to the point?
"Counsel, **where are you going with this**?" the judge asked after the fifth question about the weather.

drill.sentence: "How much do you love me? Like, on a scale of one to ten?" "Okay, {{where are you going with this}}?"
drill.hint: what are you leading up to? (not *… getting at*)

entries.related: *what are you getting at?* — suspects a hidden point; *get to the point* — an impatient demand; *what's this about?* — asks for the reason behind a request.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the speaker that you have lost track of their explanation or reasoning and need it explained again.
entries.usage: A polite, neutral way to ask for clarification in meetings, classes and conversations; it puts the problem on the listener's side, so it sounds less critical than *That doesn't make sense*. Common forms are *Sorry, I'm not following* and *I'm not following you*. Said with a frown, it can also suggest that the argument has no logic.
examples: Sorry, **I'm not following**. Why would a cheaper ticket cost us more in the end?
Wait, **I'm not following you** — is this the same Mike from your old job?
Could you go back to the second slide? **I'm not following** how you got that number.

drill.sentence: Sorry, {{I'm not following}}. Which form do I sign first, the blue one or the white one?
drill.hint: I can't keep up with your explanation (not *you lost me*, *I'm lost*, *I'm confused* or *I don't get it*)

entries.related: *I'm lost* — more casual, same idea; *I don't get it* — casual, often about a joke or a decision; *could you run that by me again?* — asks politely for a repeat.

entries.term: that's easy for you to say
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A reply saying that someone's advice or opinion costs them nothing, because they don't face the difficulty you face.
entries.usage: Common in personal conversations as a defensive reply to advice like *Just relax* or *Just quit*. It points to the other person's easier situation, so it can sound bitter; a joking tone makes it friendlier. Common variants are *Easy for you to say* and *That's easy for him to say*.
examples: "Just ask your boss for a raise." "**That's easy for you to say** — you're not on a three-month contract."
"Don't stress about the exam." "**Easy for you to say**. You graduated years ago."
The coach says the team just needs to stay calm, but that's **easy for him to say** from the sidelines.

drill.sentence: "Just stop eating sugar for a month." "{{That's easy for you to say}}. You don't even like dessert."
drill.hint: you don't face my struggle, so the advice costs you nothing

entries.related: *must be nice* — envious remark about someone's luck; *speak for yourself* — says a general claim isn't true for you; *you have no idea* — stronger, says the person can't understand.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A reply that rejects a general statement someone made about a group, saying it may be true for them but not for you.
entries.usage: A common, often joking reply when someone says *we*, *everyone* or *nobody* in a way that includes you. Said seriously, it can sound sharp. It is usually a short reply on its own, sometimes followed by your own view: *Speak for yourself — I loved it.*
examples: "We're all too old to stay out past midnight." "**Speak for yourself**! I'm just getting started."
"Nobody actually enjoys running." "**Speak for yourself** — I ran a half marathon last month."
When my brother said the whole family hated the casserole, my mom said, "**Speak for yourself**."

drill.sentence: "Everybody hates Mondays." "{{Speak for yourself}}. Monday's the only quiet day at my house."
drill.hint: that may be true for you, not for me (not *says who?*)

entries.related: *not me* — plain and neutral; *says who?* — challenges the claim itself; *you might, but I don't* — a plainer, longer version.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: An offended or defensive question that asks someone to explain a remark that seems to criticize or insult you.
entries.usage: Used in arguments between friends, couples or family when you suspect a hidden insult; in speech, *that* is usually stressed. It's confrontational, so it often starts or escalates an argument. A calmer alternative is *What do you mean by that?*
examples: "You look nice today — for once." "Wow. **What's that supposed to mean**?"
"Well, you've always been the lucky one." "Wait, **what's that supposed to mean**?"
My sister called my new haircut "brave," so I asked her **what that was supposed to mean**.

drill.sentence: "I'm sure your cooking has improved since last time." "Hey, {{what's that supposed to mean}}?"
drill.hint: offended: explain that remark (sharper than *What do you … by that?*; not *… getting at*)

entries.related: *what do you mean by that?* — a calmer request for clarification; *what are you getting at?* — asks for a hidden point, less offended; *excuse me?* — a shocked reaction to a rude remark.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that a topic annoys you so much that you could complain about it for a long time.
entries.usage: Common in casual conversation, usually as a humorous reaction when someone mentions a sore topic, with *on* + the topic. The speaker often goes on to complain anyway, which is part of the joke. *Don't even get me started* is a stronger variant, and *Don't get him started* warns others about someone else's favorite complaint.
examples: "How's the new apartment?" "Nice, but **don't get me started on** the landlord."
Airline fees? Oh, **don't get me started**. I paid forty dollars for a carry-on last week.
My dad's a retired teacher, so **don't get him started on** spelling mistakes in restaurant menus.

drill.sentence: "Did you watch the game last night?" "Ugh, {{don't get me started on}} the referees. They missed three obvious fouls."
drill.hint: this subject annoys me; I could rant for hours about

entries.related: *don't remind me* — you'd rather not think about a bad thing; *don't ask* — the story is bad or too long to tell; *a sore point* — a topic that upsets someone.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A short, often sarcastic remark that shows you envy someone's good luck or easy situation.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and online comments, as a reply on its own or as *Must be nice to* + verb. Between friends it can be teasing, but it often sounds bitter or passive-aggressive, so be careful with colleagues. The short form almost always sounds envious, while *That must be nice* can also be sincere.
examples: "My company gives us the whole week off at Christmas." "**Must be nice**."
**Must be nice** to have parents who still pay your rent.
Every time my neighbor posts photos from another beach vacation, I just think, **must be nice**.

drill.sentence: "I only work four days a week now, and I still get paid the same." "Huh. {{Must be nice}}."
drill.hint: envious reply: I wish I had that (not *lucky you* or *good for you*)

entries.related: *lucky you* — similar, sincere or sarcastic; *good for you* — usually sincere praise, sometimes sarcastic; *some of us have to work* — openly sarcastic complaint.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Says that a bad or annoying situation can't be changed, so you simply have to accept it.
entries.usage: A rhetorical question, often with a shrug or a sigh, after describing a small misfortune. It sounds resigned but calm, not angry, and no answer is expected. *What are you gonna do?* is a common casual variant.
examples: Our flight got delayed six hours. **What can you do**? We just found a good restaurant at the airport.
"Your neighbors are loud again?" "Yeah, they have a new baby. **What can you do**?"
The Mets lost again, but **what can you do**? I'll be back at the stadium next week.

drill.sentence: It snowed on the morning of our outdoor wedding, so we moved everything inside. {{What can you do}}?
drill.hint: nothing can change it, so you shrug (four words; not *oh well* or *… gonna do*)

entries.related: *it is what it is* — same acceptance, sounds flatter; *oh well* — lighter, for small problems; *that's life* — accepts bad luck as normal.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that a figure or fact seems correct, or, ironically, that a bad outcome is exactly what you expected.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and texts as a short reply, often as *That sounds about right*. In the plain sense it confirms an estimate or a detail. Said with a sigh, it means something annoying is typical of a person, company or situation.
examples: "So the repair will be around four hundred dollars?" "Yeah, that **sounds about right**."
"The cable company kept me on hold for an hour." "**Sounds about right**."
The vet says Max weighs eighty pounds, which **sounds about right** given how much he eats.

drill.sentence: "My flight was delayed again, and they lost my bag." "Yep, {{sounds about right}} for that airline."
drill.hint: that matches what I'd expect, sadly (not *figures* or *typical*)

entries.related: *figures* — sarcastic: that's what I expected; *that tracks* — it fits what I know, newer slang; *ballpark figure* — a rough estimate.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: Says that a piece of information makes sense because it fits what you already know about the person or situation.
entries.usage: Recent casual American slang, common among younger speakers and online, often with a dry, knowing tone. It comes from *track* meaning "be consistent", which also gives *That doesn't track* for a story that doesn't add up. In formal emails, *That makes sense* is safer.
examples: "Turns out she grew up on a farm." "Oh, **that tracks**. She's up at five every day."
"The guy who never tips owns three boats." "Yeah, **that tracks**."
Her excuse **doesn't track** — she said she was sick, but she posted photos from the beach.

drill.sentence: "Apparently Kevin used to be a chef." "Oh, {{that tracks}}. His lasagna is unreal."
drill.hint: that fits what I know (newer slang, not *that makes sense* or *figures*)

entries.related: *that makes sense* — neutral, fine everywhere; *figures* — sarcastic, for an annoying fact; *that adds up* — the facts fit together.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Praise for someone who noticed a mistake or a problem that others missed.
entries.usage: Very common at work, in code reviews and in everyday life; it is quick, warm praise that admits the mistake without fuss. It often goes with thanks (*Good catch, thanks!*) or with *on* + the thing noticed. *Nice catch* is used the same way.
examples: "You wrote last year's date on the invoice." "Oh, **good catch**. I'll fix it now."
"Isn't Monday a holiday? The bank will be closed." "**Good catch**. I'll deposit the check today."
**Good catch on** the allergy note. The kitchen almost put peanuts in his salad.

drill.sentence: "Wait, the recipe says teaspoons of salt, not tablespoons." "Oh, {{good catch}}! That would've been awful."
drill.hint: praise for noticing a mistake (not *nice …* or *… eye*)

entries.related: *nice catch* — same; *good eye* — praises being observant in general; *good point* — praises an argument, not a spotted error.

entries.spoken_term: take a rain check on something
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To politely say no to an invitation now while suggesting that you would like to accept it another time.
entries.usage: Very common in American English, mostly as *Can I take a rain check?* or *I'll have to take a rain check on dinner*. It sounds friendly and sincere, but if you never follow up, it becomes a polite brush-off. It comes from baseball tickets that let fans come back when a game was stopped by rain.
examples: "Want to grab a drink after work?" "I'm wiped out. Can I **take a rain check**?"
Sorry, I'll have to **take a rain check on** dinner Friday — my daughter has a fever.
He's **taken a rain check** three times now, so I've stopped inviting him.

drill.sentence: "Are you coming to the barbecue on Saturday?" "I'm on call that weekend, so I'll have to {{take a rain check}}."
drill.hint: say no for now but hope to come another time (not *pass*)

entries.related: *pass* — just declines; *maybe next time* — a lighter, vaguer promise; *raincheck* — also spelled as one word.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that you will pay for something, such as a meal or drinks, for the other people.
entries.usage: Common in restaurants, bars and coffee shops among friends and colleagues; it sounds generous and casual. Variants include *This one's on me* and *Lunch is on me*, while *It's on the house* means the business gives it for free. To insist on paying instead, people say *No, let me get this*.
examples: Order whatever you want — **it's on me** tonight.
You helped me move all weekend, so dinner's **on me**.
"What do I owe you for the tickets?" "Nothing — **this one's on me**."

drill.sentence: Don't worry about the coffee; you got lunch yesterday. {{It's on me}}.
drill.hint: the speaker is paying (not *my treat* or *I've got …*)

entries.related: *my treat* — same, slightly warmer; *I've got this* — casual, I'll pay; *it's on the house* — free, given by the business.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A modest reply to *How are you?* meaning that things are fine and there are no real problems.
entries.usage: Common in small talk with neighbors, colleagues and acquaintances; it sounds relaxed and a little understated. It is often followed by a return question such as *How about you?*, and *I can't complain* is the full form.
examples: "How's it going, Bill?" "Oh, **can't complain**. How about you?"
"How's retirement treating you?" "**Can't complain** — I golf three times a week."
"How's the new job?" "**I can't complain**. Good people, short commute."

drill.sentence: "Hey, long time no see! How are things?" "{{Can't complain}}. The kids are healthy, and work's steady."
drill.hint: modest reply meaning things are fine (not *not bad*, *pretty good* or *could be worse*)

entries.related: *not bad* — similar, very common; *could be worse* — a little more negative; *never better* — enthusiastic.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: Means that a long time has passed since something last happened, especially since you last saw someone.
entries.usage: Casual American slang, now very common, especially among younger speakers; the *minute* is ironic and means a long time. It's natural when greeting friends or texting. In formal settings or from someone who doesn't usually use slang, it can sound forced.
examples: Jess! Wow, **it's been a minute** — how have you been?
**It's been a minute** since I've ridden a bike, so go easy on me.
"When did you last visit your parents?" "Honestly, **it's been a minute**."

drill.sentence: Hey, stranger! {{It's been a minute}}. Did you move or something?
drill.hint: a long time has passed (slangy, not *… a while*, *ages* or *long time no see*)

entries.related: *it's been a while* — neutral; *long time no see* — a casual greeting; *it's been ages* — more emphatic.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A casual way to thank someone for a favor and say that you will do something for them in return.
entries.usage: Common among friends, neighbors and colleagues after a practical favor, like covering a shift or giving a ride. It's warm and informal; for a big favor people say *I owe you big time*. The reply is often *Don't mention it* or a joke like *I'll hold you to that*.
examples: Thanks for picking up the kids today. **I owe you one**.
"I covered your shift on Saturday." "Seriously? **I owe you one**."
She fixed my resume the night before the interview, so **I owe her one**.

drill.sentence: You're driving me to the airport at five in the morning? Wow, {{I owe you one}}.
drill.hint: thanks — I'll return the favor someday (four words)

entries.related: *I owe you big time* — stronger; *you're a lifesaver* — thanks for urgent help; *I'll return the favor* — more neutral and explicit.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells listeners to ignore what you just said, because you are correcting it or changing your mind.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, meetings and voice messages, said right before the correction, often after *actually* or *no*. It sounds quick and casual, not embarrassed. In writing, people simply delete the error, so it appears mainly in chatty texts.
examples: Let's meet at the café at noon — no, **scratch that**, one o'clock.
We'll need eight chairs. **Scratch that** — Kim's bringing her boyfriend, so nine.
Okay, the deadline is Thursday. Actually, **scratch that**: the client moved it to Monday.

drill.sentence: Grab some milk on your way home. Actually, {{scratch that}}, I just found a carton in the back of the fridge.
drill.hint: ignore what I just said (two words; not *never mind* or *forget …*)

entries.related: *never mind* — drop the request completely; *let me rephrase* — say it better, not change it; *strike that* — more formal, also used in court.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Means "according to the most recent information I have"; it is often used sarcastically to point out something obvious.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and online arguments, at the start or the end of a sentence. Used sincerely, it adds a small hedge; used sarcastically, it reminds someone of an obvious fact they seem to ignore. *Last time I checked* means the same.
examples: Why am I always the one doing the dishes? **Last I checked**, you live here too.
**Last I checked**, the pool was closed for repairs, but call them to make sure.
You can't tell us to leave. This is a public park, **last I checked**.

drill.sentence: "You should cook dinner tonight." "Why me? {{Last I checked}}, it's your turn."
drill.hint: according to my latest info — said with sarcasm (three words; not *as far as I know*)

entries.related: *as far as I know* — a sincere hedge, no sarcasm; *in case you forgot* — openly sarcastic; *last time I looked* — same, a bit longer.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces the first of several reasons or points, often in a complaint or an argument.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, usually when listing problems or reasons against something. It suggests that more points will follow, so it can sound critical or impatient. *To start with* is similar, and *first of all* is more neutral.
examples: "What's wrong with the apartment?" "Well, **for starters**, there's no hot water."
I'm not buying that car. **For starters**, it's way too expensive, and the mileage is terrible.
The new coach has a lot to fix, but **for starters**, the team has to stop giving up late goals.

drill.sentence: "Why don't you want to go camping?" "Well, {{for starters}}, it's supposed to rain all weekend."
drill.hint: my first reason, with more to come (not *first of all*, *first off*, *to begin with* or *for one thing*)

entries.related: *for one thing* — gives one reason, often followed by *for another*; *first of all* — neutral, any first point; *to begin with* — a little more formal.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that your words sounded ruder or different from what you meant, and you want to correct the impression.
entries.usage: Said right after an awkward remark, often with a quick laugh, among friends, family or colleagues. It takes responsibility for the wording, unlike *I didn't mean it like that*, which answers someone's reaction. It is usually followed by a better version: *That came out wrong — what I meant was …*
examples: You look great for your age — wait, **that came out wrong**.
"So you're saying my cooking is boring?" "No! Sorry, **that came out wrong**. I meant it's simple."
**That came out wrong** in my email; I wasn't blaming your team for the delay.

drill.sentence: Wow, you're so much nicer than your sister. Oh no, {{that came out wrong}}. I just meant you're easier to talk to.
drill.hint: my words sounded ruder than I meant (not *I didn't mean it like that*)

entries.related: *I didn't mean it like that* — says the listener misunderstood you; *let me rephrase* — neutral, offers a clearer version; *poor choice of words* — admits the wording was bad, more formal.

entries.term: I didn't mean it like that
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that someone has understood your words in a more negative way than you intended.
entries.usage: Used when someone reacts badly to something you said, in personal conversations and sometimes at work. It defends your intention, so after a real insult it can sound like an excuse; an apology helps: *Sorry, I didn't mean it like that.* *I didn't mean it that way* is a common variant.
examples: "So you think I'm lazy?" "No, **I didn't mean it like that**. You just seem tired."
When I called his plan ambitious, he got upset, but **I didn't mean it like that**.
Sorry, **I didn't mean it like that** — I love the gift, I just already have one.

drill.sentence: "You think I'm too old to go back to school?" "No, no, {{I didn't mean it like that}}. I think it's great."
drill.hint: you took my words the wrong way (not *that came out wrong* or *that's not what I meant*)

entries.related: *that came out wrong* — admits your wording was bad; *that's not what I meant* — corrects the meaning, a bit more neutral; *don't take this the wrong way* — said before a remark, to prevent offense.

entries.term: I hate to break it to you, but …
entries.spoken_term: I hate to break it to you, but
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces disappointing news or an unwelcome truth that the listener does not know or does not want to accept.
entries.usage: Common in casual conversation; it can be truly sympathetic, but it is often teasing or slightly condescending when the truth is obvious. *Break the news to someone* is the related neutral phrase. In professional emails, *Unfortunately, …* is safer.
examples: **I hate to break it to you, but** the concert's been sold out for weeks.
"I'll be able to retire at fifty." "**I hate to break it to you, but** not with that much credit card debt."
Look, **I hate to break it to you**, but your team isn't making the playoffs this year.

drill.sentence: {{I hate to break it to you, but}} the taco place you keep talking about closed last month.
drill.hint: an apologetic lead-in to unwelcome news (not *unfortunately* or *sorry to tell you*)

entries.related: *sorry to be the bearer of bad news* — similar, a little more formal; *news flash* — sarcastic, points out something obvious; *the bad news is* — neutral.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a critical or rude remark while claiming that you don't intend to hurt the listener.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, but it rarely softens much: listeners often hear it as a warning that an insult is coming, so it can sound passive-aggressive. Among friends it is often used jokingly, and the reply *None taken* can be sincere or sarcastic. The American spelling is *offense*.
examples: **No offense, but** your car smells like old french fries.
**No offense, but** I don't think you're the right person to give relationship advice.
I love your brother, **no offense**, but he never stops talking about crypto.

drill.sentence: {{No offense, but}} that hat makes you look like a detective from an old movie.
drill.hint: please don't be upset by my criticism (not *don't take this the wrong way* or *not to be rude*)

entries.related: *don't take this the wrong way* — softer, similar; *with all due respect* — formal, before disagreeing; *I don't mean to be rude, but* — softens a remark that might seem impolite.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A formal phrase that introduces a disagreement or criticism, especially toward someone senior, while claiming to stay respectful.
entries.usage: Used in meetings, interviews, hearings and serious discussions, followed by a strong objection; *with all due respect to* + person is also common. In practice it often signals that a blunt disagreement is coming, and in heated talk it can sound sarcastic. Avoid it with friends unless you're joking.
examples: **With all due respect**, sir, the numbers don't support that decision.
**With all due respect to** the school board, nobody asked parents about the new start times.
"Just trust me, I'm your doctor." "**With all due respect**, I'd like a second opinion."

drill.sentence: {{With all due respect}}, Coach, I've played this position for six years, and I know what I'm doing.
drill.hint: formal, polite lead-in to disagreeing with someone senior (not *no offense* or *respectfully*)

entries.related: *respectfully* — shorter, similar; *no offense, but* — casual, before a personal criticism; *I take your point, but* — accepts an argument before disagreeing.

entries.term: I don't mean to be rude, but …
entries.spoken_term: I don't mean to be rude, but
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a request, question or remark that might seem impolite, to show you know it could cause offense.
entries.usage: Common when you need to interrupt, refuse, ask a personal question or end a conversation. It is softer than *no offense, but*, which usually comes before a personal criticism. Like it, though, it can sound passive-aggressive if a real insult follows.
examples: Excuse me, **I don't mean to be rude, but** I was next in line.
He kept talking, so finally I said, "**I don't mean to be rude, but** I have a train to catch."
**I don't mean to be rude, but** could you lower your voice a little? My baby's asleep.

drill.sentence: {{I don't mean to be rude, but}} you're sitting in my seat. My ticket says window.
drill.hint: a softener before a remark that may sound impolite (not *excuse me*, *no offense* or *not to be …*)

entries.related: *no offense, but* — before a criticism; *excuse me, but* — a polite interruption; *not to be rude, but* — shorter, same idea.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a statement that you want people to clearly know or remember, often to correct a wrong idea or to protect yourself later.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, arguments and interviews, at the start or the end of a sentence. It sounds firm and sometimes defensive, as if you want your position noted before things go wrong. Literally, it also means "to be written in the official record", as in court or in a meeting's minutes.
examples: **For the record**, I said this restaurant was a bad idea.
I'm happy to help, but **for the record**, this is the last time I'm lending him money.
The witness said, **for the record**, that she had never seen the man before.

drill.sentence: {{For the record}}, I wasn't the one who left the front door unlocked last night.
drill.hint: so it's clearly noted (not *just so you know* or *to be clear*)

entries.related: *just so you know* — informs, less formal; *to be clear* — prevents misunderstanding; *off the record* — the opposite: not to be quoted.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces an honest admission, often something slightly surprising or embarrassing about yourself.
entries.usage: Used in conversation and in personal writing; it sounds a little literary compared with *to be honest*. It usually introduces a personal confession or an unexpected opinion, and it can start the sentence or follow *but*.
examples: Everyone loved the movie, but **truth be told**, I fell asleep halfway through.
**Truth be told**, I only took the job because of the free gym.
The team won the title, but, **truth be told**, they got lucky in the semifinal.

drill.sentence: I told everyone I'd miss the city, but {{truth be told}}, I love the quiet out here.
drill.hint: here's my confession (a literary three-word phrase, not *to be honest* or *to tell you …*)

entries.related: *to be honest* — the everyday version; *if I'm being honest* — softer, very common; *the truth is* — similar, more direct.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a fact about your own connection or interest, such as a friendship or money, that might make your opinion biased.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, reviews, journalism and online posts, usually at the start and often followed by a colon in writing. It sounds open and fair-minded, and people also use it humorously for small personal biases. In journalism and research, the formal term is a *conflict of interest*.
examples: **Full disclosure**: the owner is my cousin, but honestly, it's the best bagel shop in town.
**Full disclosure**, I own some shares in the company, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.
In the interest of **full disclosure**, I should mention that I used to date the bride.

drill.sentence: {{Full disclosure}}: I'm a lifelong Yankees fan, so I'm not exactly neutral about tonight's game.
drill.hint: telling you my bias up front (not *for the record*)

entries.related: *for the record* — makes a statement clearly known; *I should mention* — plainer; *conflict of interest* — the formal term for such a bias.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces an unpleasant or uncomfortable fact that everyone should admit is true.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, opinion pieces and speeches, usually at the start of a sentence. It sounds frank and slightly blunt, and it invites the listener to agree. It's informal enough to sound out of place in formal reports.
examples: I love the old house, but **let's face it**, it needs a new roof and new wiring.
**Let's face it**: we're not going to finish this puzzle tonight.
**Let's face it**, most people only read the headline, not the article.

drill.sentence: We can keep blaming the weather, but {{let's face it}}, we just didn't play well tonight.
drill.hint: we must admit the uncomfortable truth (not *… be honest* or *… be real*)

entries.related: *let's be honest* — similar, slightly softer; *face it* — shorter, more direct, addressed to one person; *the truth is* — neutral.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a careful estimate or opinion: *I think, roughly* or *in my view*.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and at work, especially before numbers and judgments. The *would* makes the claim softer and less certain than *I think*. It often answers a question, and it can also follow the estimate: *Fifty, I'd say.*
examples: "How many people were at the party?" "**I'd say** around sixty, maybe more."
**I'd say** she's in her late thirties, but it's hard to tell.
Honestly, **I'd say** the second apartment is the better deal.

drill.sentence: "How far is it to the lake?" "{{I'd say}} about twenty minutes, if there's no traffic."
drill.hint: my rough estimate is (not *I think*, *I guess* or *I'd guess*)

entries.related: *I think* — more direct; *I'd guess* — even less sure; *roughly* / *about* — mark the number itself as approximate.

entries.term: as far as I can tell
entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Means that your statement is based only on what you have seen or understood so far, and you might be missing something.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, emails and technical discussions; it hedges a conclusion you are fairly sure about. It can start or end the sentence. Compare *as far as I know*, which is about information you have heard or learned, not what you have observed.
examples: **As far as I can tell**, the rattling noise is coming from the dryer.
She seems happy at her new school, **as far as I can tell**.
**As far as I can tell**, the bug only appears when two people edit the same file.

drill.sentence: The dog seems fine after eating the sock, {{as far as I can tell}}, but I'll call the vet just in case.
drill.hint: based on what I've observed (not *as far as I know* or *from what I can …*)

entries.related: *as far as I know* — based on what you have heard or learned; *from what I can see* — very similar; *apparently* — based on what others say.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces information you have heard from other people, without claiming you know it for sure.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often about other people, places or plans. It marks the information as secondhand, so it is a polite way to pass on news or gossip. Variants include *from what I've heard* and *I hear (that)*.
examples: **From what I hear**, the new Thai place on Elm Street is amazing.
"Is Dave still with Emma?" "Not anymore, **from what I hear**."
**From what I've heard**, the city plans to close the bridge for repairs all summer.

drill.sentence: I haven't met their new baby yet, but {{from what I hear}}, she doesn't sleep at all.
drill.hint: according to other people's reports (not *apparently* or *rumor has it*)

entries.related: *apparently* — similar, one word; *rumor has it* — for gossip, more playful; *as far as I can tell* — based on your own observation.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces an impression you have formed from someone's behavior or a situation, without clear proof.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, often about people's feelings or intentions. It sounds tentative and perceptive, which makes it useful for raising a sensitive observation gently. *That* is often dropped, and the past *I got the sense* and the progressive *I'm getting the sense* are common too.
examples: **I get the sense that** he's not really interested in the job.
**I'm getting the sense** you'd rather not talk about it, and that's okay.
From the way she answered the phone, I **got the sense that** something was wrong at home.

drill.sentence: {{I get the sense that}} the kids aren't telling us everything about the broken window.
drill.hint: my impression is (not *I get the feeling/impression*, *I suspect* or *something tells me*)

entries.related: *I have a feeling* — more about intuition; *I get the impression* — very similar; *something tells me* — a hunch, often playful.

entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: A polite hedge that presents a fact you are quite sure of, while leaving room to be corrected.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, formal conversations and polite corrections, at the start, middle or end of a sentence. It is often used to correct someone gently, and said firmly it sounds confident rather than unsure. It is more formal than *I think*.
examples: **If I'm not mistaken**, you two went to the same high school.
The museum is free on Thursdays, **if I'm not mistaken**.
"Was this your idea?" "Actually, **if I'm not mistaken**, it was yours."

drill.sentence: That's Julia's car in the driveway, {{if I'm not mistaken}}. I thought she was out of town.
drill.hint: I'm fairly sure, but I could be off (not *unless …* or *if I remember …*)

entries.related: *if I remember correctly* — for memories; *correct me if I'm wrong* — similar, invites correction more openly; *I believe* — plainer.

entries.term: for lack of a better word
entries.label: hedging phrase
entries.meaning: Admits that the word you are using is not exactly right, but it is the best one you can find.
entries.usage: Common in speech and informal writing, placed just before or after the imperfect word, often between commas. It sounds thoughtful and is sometimes used for humor, before a word that is too polite or too strong. *For lack of a better term* is a variant, and *for want of a better word* is more formal and more British.
examples: The party was, **for lack of a better word**, weird.
My grandpa had a, **for lack of a better word**, creative relationship with the truth.
**For lack of a better term**, their new office feels like a playground for adults.

drill.sentence: His new girlfriend is, {{for lack of a better word}}, intense — she's already planning their wedding.
drill.hint: my chosen term isn't quite right, but it's the closest I can find (not *for want of …* or *let's say*)

entries.related: *for want of a better word* — same, more formal; *so to speak* — marks a word as not literal; *if you will* — similar, a bit formal.

entries.term: I'm not sure that's quite right
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite, indirect way of telling someone that what they said is wrong.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, classes and professional conversations, especially with people you don't know well or who are senior. The hedges *not sure* and *quite* soften the correction, but most listeners understand it as a clear *no*. It usually needs a reason or the correct information after it.
examples: Hmm, **I'm not sure that's quite right** — I think the store closes at nine, not ten.
**I'm not sure that's quite right**, Dr. Lee. The scan was taken before the surgery.
"Didn't the Romans build the pyramids?" "Um, **I'm not sure that's quite right**."

drill.sentence: "So the meeting moved to Thursday?" "Sorry, {{I'm not sure that's quite right}}. I think it's still on Wednesday."
drill.hint: a very polite, hedged way to say you're wrong (not *I don't think …*)

entries.related: *I don't think that's right* — more direct; *that's not quite it* — casual; *actually, …* — a common, short way to start a correction.

entries.term: it's not the end of the world
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that a problem is disappointing or annoying but not serious, usually to comfort someone or yourself.
entries.usage: Very common when reassuring someone about a small failure or setback. It sounds supportive, but said to someone who is very upset it can seem dismissive. It also appears as *it wouldn't be the end of the world if …* and *it won't be the end of the world*.
examples: So you failed your driving test. **It's not the end of the world** — you can take it again next month.
If we don't get this house, **it won't be the end of the world**; there are others.
Losing the first game **isn't the end of the world** — the season is long.

drill.sentence: Okay, so the cake's a little lopsided. {{It's not the end of the world}}. Nobody will care once they taste it.
drill.hint: it's bad, but not a disaster (not *no big deal*)

entries.related: *no big deal* — says it's not important at all; *it could be worse* — compares with a worse outcome; *these things happen* — comfort after an accident.
